title: The Road So Far, and the Road Ahead
summary: The car was not invented by one person, but by thousands of clever people over 250 years, from a steam wagon slower than walking to robot taxis. Cars gave us amazing freedom, but also crashes, smog and traffic jams. Now it's your turn to imagine the car of the future!

sections.heading: Rewind: 250 Years in One Drive
paragraphs: Let's take one last drive together, but this time through time instead of space. Imagine a road that begins in 1770 and ends today. Every few kilometres there is a signpost with a date, and beside each signpost stands a machine. Shall we go?

Our first stop is Paris in 1770. Here stands Nicolas-Joseph Cugnot's fardier, a huge three-wheeled steam wagon built for the French army to haul cannons. Its great copper boiler hangs out in front like the nose of a dragon. It moves at about 4 kilometres per hour, no faster than you walk, and it must stop every quarter of an hour or so to build up steam. But it moves by itself. For the first time, a full-size road vehicle is pushing itself along without a horse, an ox or a person pulling.

Next signpost: Mannheim, Germany, 1886. Karl Benz has just applied for patent number 37435 for his Patent-Motorwagen, a light three-wheeler with a small petrol engine of less than one horsepower. Unlike earlier inventors who bolted engines onto carriages, Benz designed the whole vehicle around its engine. People often call this patent the 'birth certificate' of the automobile.

Two years later, in August 1888, we spot Bertha Benz rattling down a country lane with her teenage sons Eugen and Richard, on the way to her mother's house in Pforzheim, about 106 kilometres away. She buys fuel at a pharmacy, fixes problems with whatever she has to hand, and arrives by dusk. Her journey proves to the world, and to her worried husband, that a car can make a real trip.

The road now crosses the Atlantic. On 1 October 1908, Ford's Model T goes on sale: tough, simple and high off the ground for bumpy country roads. In 1913, at the Highland Park factory in Michigan, Ford's team starts using a moving assembly line. Within about a year, the time to put together a Model T chassis drops from around twelve and a half hours to about an hour and a half. Prices tumble, and millions of ordinary families buy their first car. By 1927, more than 15 million Model Ts have been built.

Between those signposts the road itself changes beneath our wheels. Muddy tracks become tarmac. In 1932 Germany opens its first autobahn section between Cologne and Bonn, and in 1956 the United States begins building its giant Interstate highway system. Traffic lights blink at crossroads, petrol stations appear on street corners, and families pile into their cars for holidays, drive-in films and new homes in the suburbs. Racing drivers chase records on closed tracks such as Brooklands and Indianapolis, and the lessons they learn about brakes and tyres find their way into ordinary cars. But the road also grows more dangerous and more polluted, and by the 1960s people are demanding safer, cleaner cars.

Further along, in 1959, we pass a Volvo, and inside is a new kind of seatbelt designed by engineer Nils Bohlin: the three-point belt, which crosses both the hips and the chest. Volvo lets other carmakers use the design for free, and it goes on to save, by Volvo's estimate, more than a million lives.

Then the road fills with quiet humming. From 2008, when the Tesla Roadster appears, followed by the Nissan Leaf in 2010 and many others, electric cars make their great comeback, powered by lithium-ion batteries. Remember that electric cars were not new at all; around 1900 they were popular in many cities before petrol cars took over.

Our last signpost reads 2020. In the sunny suburbs of Phoenix, Arizona, a car pulls up with nobody in the driver's seat. Waymo's fully driverless taxis are open to the public. From walking pace in 1770 to robot taxis in 2020 took about 250 years. Along the way, the fastest car on Earth went from about 4 km/h to about 1,228 km/h, the speed reached by the jet-powered ThrustSSC in 1997 when it became the first car to break the sound barrier.

sections.heading: Not One Inventor, but a Relay Race
paragraphs: If someone asks you, 'Who invented the car?', what should you say? After twenty parts, you know the honest answer is: thousands of people. The car was not invented in one flash of genius. It was more like a relay race, with each runner carrying the baton a little further and then handing it on.

Cugnot showed that a machine could move a vehicle. Étienne Lenoir built the first commercially successful internal combustion engine in 1860. Alphonse Beau de Rochas described the four-stroke idea on paper in 1862, and Nicolaus Otto built a working four-stroke engine in 1876. Gottlieb Daimler and Wilhelm Maybach made engines light and fast enough to fit in a vehicle. Karl Benz built and patented the first practical automobile powered by an internal combustion engine. Bertha Benz proved it worked over a long distance.

Then came the problem-solvers. Robert William Thomson and John Boyd Dunlop gave us air-filled tyres, and the Michelin brothers put them on cars. Robert Bosch's company and engineer Gottlob Honold gave engines a reliable spark. Rudolf Diesel found a way to ignite fuel by squeezing air until it was hot. Charles Kettering's electric self-starter, first offered on the 1912 Cadillac, meant nobody had to risk a broken wrist turning a hand crank. Malcolm Loughead's hydraulic brakes helped cars stop safely.

Others built the world around the car. John Loudon McAdam and Edgar Purnell Hooley improved road surfaces. Traffic engineers, from John Peake Knight in 1868 London to the designers of electric signals in American cities, invented ways to control traffic. Garrett Morgan patented an improved traffic signal. Mary Anderson patented a windscreen wiper. Béla Barényi invented the crumple zone, and Nils Bohlin perfected the three-point seatbelt.

And still others changed how cars were made and sold. Ransom Olds built cars in large numbers. Ford's engineers, including Charles Sorensen, combined older ideas into the moving assembly line. Alfred Sloan at General Motors offered a car 'for every purse and purpose'. Taiichi Ohno at Toyota found ways to build cars with less waste. Scientists such as John Goodenough, Stanley Whittingham and Akira Yoshino developed the lithium-ion battery, and computer scientists like Ernst Dickmanns and Sebastian Thrun taught cars to see.

These people came from France, Germany, Britain, Belgium, Austria, Hungary, Sweden, the United States, Japan and many other countries. Some were famous; many more were factory workers, mechanics, test drivers and inventors whose names nobody remembers. And many of them worked on just one small piece of the puzzle. That is how most big inventions really happen. A great idea is rarely a lone hero's triumph. It is a team effort stretched across time and across the world.

sections.heading: The Great Trade-Off
paragraphs: Cars have given people something wonderful: freedom. A family can visit grandparents in another town on a Sunday afternoon. A doctor can reach a farmhouse in the middle of the night. Fresh food, medicines and parcels arrive at shops and homes. In many countries, getting a driving licence feels like a ticket to growing up. Before cars, most people rarely travelled more than a day's walk or horse ride from home. Today, a car can carry you hundreds of kilometres between breakfast and lunch.
But every one of the stories in this Deep Dive also showed a cost, and we still argue today about how to balance the good and the bad.

The first cost is safety. According to the World Health Organization, road traffic crashes kill about 1.2 million people every year around the world, and they are the leading cause of death for children and young people aged 5 to 29. More than half of those killed are pedestrians, cyclists and motorcyclists, the people least protected by steel and airbags. About nine in ten road deaths happen in low- and middle-income countries, even though those countries have only around 60 percent of the world's vehicles. The good news is that safety ideas work. In many wealthy countries, the number of deaths for every kilometre driven has fallen enormously since the 1960s, thanks to seatbelts, crumple zones, airbags, better roads and laws against drink-driving. The United Nations has set the goal of cutting road deaths and injuries in half by 2030.

The second cost is pollution. Exhaust fumes cause smog and harm people's lungs, and burning petrol or diesel releases carbon dioxide, the main gas driving climate change. Cars and vans together produce roughly a tenth of all the world's energy-related carbon dioxide, and cars burn a large share of the world's oil. Leaded petrol was finally removed worldwide in 2021, a reminder that serious mistakes can be fixed, even if it takes a long time.

The third cost is space. There are now roughly one and a half billion motor vehicles in the world, and some estimates are even higher. Every one of them needs a place to park, by many estimates for more than 90 percent of the day, when it is just sitting still. In many cities, huge areas of land are covered by car parks, wide roads and motorway junctions, land that could have been parks, homes or playgrounds. Traffic jams waste time and fuel; drivers in big cities can lose days every year sitting in queues.

The fourth cost is harder to measure: what cars do to communities. When cities are built mainly for cars, shops spread out along busy roads, children have fewer safe places to walk or cycle, and people who cannot drive, because they are too young, too old, or cannot afford a car, can find it hard to get around.

None of this means cars are bad. It means that, like every powerful invention, they come with trade-offs. The interesting question for the future is not 'cars or no cars?' but 'how can we keep the freedom and lose as much of the harm as possible?'

sections.heading: Better Batteries and Cars That Get Reborn
paragraphs: Let's start our look into the future with the part that matters most for electric cars: the battery. Today's electric cars use lithium-ion batteries. Inside each cell, tiny charged particles called lithium ions travel back and forth between two layers, through a liquid called the electrolyte. That liquid works well, but it can catch fire if the battery is badly damaged or overheats, and it limits how much energy can be packed in.

Many scientists and carmakers are working on solid-state batteries, which swap the liquid electrolyte for a solid one, such as a special ceramic or a solid plastic-like material. In theory, solid-state batteries could store more energy in the same weight, letting a car go further on a charge. Because most solid electrolytes do not burn, they could also be safer, and some designs might charge much faster. In 2023 the electronics company Panasonic reported a small solid-state prototype that could charge from 10 to 80 percent in about three minutes.

But making them is hard. Thin, spiky threads of lithium metal, called dendrites, can grow through the electrolyte and cause short circuits. The solid layers must stay pressed tightly together even as the battery swells and shrinks during charging. And manufacturing them cheaply in huge numbers has not yet been achieved. Toyota, which holds thousands of solid-state battery patents, has said it does not expect to use them in commercial cars before about 2027, and other carmakers such as Nissan, Honda, BMW and Hyundai are aiming for the late 2020s or the 2030s. Plenty of companies have announced breakthroughs; the real test is whether those batteries can be made by the million at a fair price.

Meanwhile, ordinary lithium-ion batteries keep improving. They have become far cheaper over the past fifteen years, and new chemistries, such as lithium iron phosphate (often shortened to LFP), avoid using cobalt, a metal whose mining has raised serious concerns about pollution and the treatment of workers. Some researchers are also working on sodium-ion batteries, which use sodium, the same element found in table salt, instead of scarcer lithium.

Batteries are not the only possible path. Some carmakers are still developing hydrogen fuel-cell cars, which make electricity on board by combining hydrogen with oxygen from the air and give off only water vapour. They can be refuelled in a few minutes, but hydrogen is costly to make cleanly and there are very few filling stations. Others are experimenting with fuels made from plants or waste, or even from captured carbon dioxide and clean electricity, which might one day keep older petrol cars, ships and aircraft running with less harm to the climate. Engineers do not yet agree on which mix of ideas will win; most likely, different solutions will suit different jobs.

The future car might also have a second life, and a third. Cars are already among the most recycled products in the world. When a car reaches the end of its life, workers drain its fluids and remove its battery, tyres and catalytic converter. Then the rest is crushed and shredded, and magnets and other machines sort out the metals. About three quarters of the material in a typical car can be recycled, and old cars supply millions of tonnes of steel to steelworks every year. Recycling metal uses far less energy than digging up and processing new ore.

Electric car batteries are the next big recycling challenge. An old battery that can no longer power a car well may still be useful for years storing electricity from solar panels, a so-called 'second life'. After that, recycling plants can recover valuable metals like lithium, nickel and cobalt to make new batteries. Engineers dream of a 'circular' car industry, where the materials in today's cars become the cars of tomorrow, over and over again.

sections.heading: Shared Robot Taxis and Cities for People
paragraphs: Now imagine a city street in the year 2050. What do you see? Nobody knows for certain, but here is one possible picture that many planners talk about.

Fewer people own their own cars. Instead, when you need a ride, you tap an app and a clean, quiet electric robotaxi arrives. It drops you off and drives away to pick up the next passenger, rather than sitting in a car park all day. If one shared car can do the work of several privately owned ones, a city might need far fewer parking spaces. Old car parks could become parks, homes, sports fields or gardens.

In this picture, streets look different too. Wide lanes are narrowed to make space for trees, benches, bicycle paths and wider pavements. Buses and trams run often and on time. Children can walk or cycle to school safely, as many did before city streets were filled with cars. Some cities, such as Pontevedra in Spain, have already turned much of their centres into areas mostly for people on foot, and cities including Paris and Amsterdam have built hundreds of kilometres of cycle lanes.

But there is another possible picture, and experts warn about it. If robotaxis become very cheap and comfortable, people might take more car trips, not fewer, instead of walking, cycling or catching a bus. Empty robot cars could drive around looking for passengers, adding to traffic. So whether self-driving cars make cities better or worse depends not just on the technology, but on the choices people and governments make: how roads are shared, how rides are priced, and how much space is given to public transport.

There are smaller changes coming as well. Cars are becoming computers on wheels, connected to the internet and updated with new software, a bit like a phone. Some may 'talk' to traffic lights and to each other, warning of an icy patch or a crash around the next bend. Electric cars could even help run the electricity grid, charging when there is lots of wind and solar power and, in some systems, sending power back when it is needed. All of these ideas have to be designed carefully to keep people's information private and to keep cars safe from hackers.

sections.heading: Cars That Fly? Electric Air Taxis
paragraphs: For about a hundred years, people have dreamed of flying cars, and cartoons and comics are full of them. They have always been held back by the same problems: they are noisy, expensive, need a lot of power and are hard to fly safely over crowded cities. Now a new kind of machine is getting close to carrying passengers: the eVTOL, short for 'electric vertical take-off and landing' aircraft.

An eVTOL is not really a car. It is more like a quiet electric helicopter with many small propellers, each spun by its own electric motor. Computers constantly adjust each propeller to keep the aircraft steady. Because electric motors are simple and there are many of them, if one fails the others can keep flying. Companies such as Joby Aviation and Archer Aviation in the United States, Volocopter in Germany and EHang in China have built eVTOLs and tested them in many flights. In October 2023, China's aviation authority gave EHang's EH216-S, a two-seat aircraft designed to fly without a pilot on board, a type certificate, a key step towards carrying passengers.

The idea is to use eVTOLs as air taxis, hopping over traffic jams from rooftops or special 'vertiports' to airports or across a city in a few minutes. But they face the same challenge as electric cars, only much harder. Batteries are heavy, and an aircraft has to lift its own weight into the air, so range is limited. Safety rules for aircraft are very strict, as they should be, and every new type must pass long certification tests. Cities will also have to decide where these aircraft may fly and land, and how much noise people will accept. Air taxis may become one more option for travel, but for a long time to come most journeys will still happen on the ground.

sections.heading: Back to Bertha, and Forward to You
paragraphs: Let's finish where so much of this story began: on a dusty country road in Germany, early one August morning in 1888.

Bertha Benz grips the steering tiller of the Motorwagen. Her sons are beside and behind her, ready to jump out and push on the hills. Nobody has ever driven a car this far before. There are no filling stations, no garages, no road signs for drivers, and no mechanics who have ever seen a machine like this. When the fuel runs low, she stops at a pharmacy in Wiesloch to buy a cleaning fluid called ligroin. When problems strike, according to the family's story, she uses a hatpin and a garter to fix them, and a shoemaker nails leather onto the brakes. By the end of the day, against all expectations, she has arrived. Today you can follow her route yourself: the Bertha Benz Memorial Route, opened in 2008, winds through the towns she passed, from Mannheim through Wiesloch and Bruchsal to Pforzheim.

Why does this scene matter so much? Because Bertha did not wait for everything to be perfect. She saw that the car worked well enough to try, and she went out and solved the problems one at a time as they appeared. When she got home, she told Karl what needed improving, such as an extra low gear for climbing hills, and the next version was better. That is how engineering works: try, learn, improve, try again.

The road ahead has big problems of its own. How do we make all the electricity for electric cars from clean sources like sun, wind and water? How do we bring road deaths closer to zero, especially for people walking and cycling? How do we make batteries without harming people or nature, and recycle every part of a car? How do we design cities where cars are useful but do not crowd out everything else? Who will make sure self-driving cars are safe and fair to everyone?

Nobody has fully solved these problems yet. That is exciting news, because it means there is work for the next generation of inventors, engineers, scientists, designers, city planners and lawmakers. Some of the people who will solve them are kids right now, reading about Cugnot's steam wagon and Bertha's daring drive and wondering, 'How could that be done better?'

Remember the patterns from this long story. Big inventions are built by many people, so it is fine to work on one small piece. Every invention has trade-offs, so think about who is helped and who might be harmed. Testing honestly matters, so never hide a problem. And curiosity, plus a bit of courage, can carry an idea a very long way, just as it carried Bertha all the way to Pforzheim.

So grab a pencil and a sheet of paper. What would your car of the future look like? Would it run on sunlight, fold up to fit in a cupboard, carry a whole football team, or not be a car at all? The road ahead is open, and the next chapter of this story is waiting for you to design it.

deepDive: Historians of technology often use the automobile as their favourite example of 'systems' thinking. A car on its own is useless; it needs fuel supplies, repair shops, paved roads, traffic laws, driving tests, insurance, finance, factories and a workforce trained to build it. The historian Thomas Hughes called these 'large technical systems', and they explain why the car took decades to spread even after the Benz patent of 1886: the system around it had to be built too. The same lesson applies to electric and self-driving cars today. Battery chemistry is only one piece; charging networks, grid capacity, mining and recycling, insurance law and new safety standards must all grow at the same time. Another idea historians stress is 'path dependence': choices made early can lock in later ones. The petrol engine won around 1910 partly because of cheap Texas oil, the electric starter and the low price of the Model T, not because it was best in every way. Once cities, petrol stations and repair skills were built around it, switching became very expensive, which is one reason the electric comeback took a century. Debates about the future often divide between technological optimists and those who emphasise behaviour and planning. Optimists point to the roughly 90% fall in battery prices since 2010 and to robotaxis already carrying paying passengers. Sceptics point to the 'rebound effect' (when something becomes cheaper and easier, people use more of it, so cheap robotaxis could increase total traffic) and to the fact that an electric car's climate benefit depends on how the electricity and the battery are made. Most studies find electric cars produce lower lifetime emissions than petrol cars in most countries, with the gap growing as grids get cleaner, but the size of that gap varies a lot from place to place. Finally, transport researchers note that the safest, cleanest trip is often the one not made by car at all: well-designed public transport, walking and cycling are part of any serious plan for healthier, lower-carbon cities. The future of the car will therefore be decided by engineers and also by voters, planners and everyday travellers.
funFact: By many estimates, most privately owned cars spend more than 90 percent of their lives parked, which is why some planners think shared robotaxis could free up huge amounts of city land.
